correctness.rationale: For each vaccinated path vertex, unique-path connectivity yields M=1+2[F(a)+F(b)]/(n-1), with strictly increasing discrete increments of F. A first secondary infection occurs iff an incident residual edge is open, so R=[L(a)+L(b)]/(n-1), where L counts endpoints and internal vertices. Exact positive differences p², 2p-p² force distinct risk minimizers, while discrete convexity forces central mean minimizers. All trees of size at most four are paths or a star, and the star center minimizes both. An independently written rational bond-configuration enumerator reproduces both identities and all optimizer sets at 162 test cases; this finite test does not prove the all-n statement.

originality.rationale: The 2015 original article already motivates the difference between mean-based and tail-based vaccination goals; that broad qualitative distinction is not claimed as new. The narrower complete universal-in-p optimizer theorem for independent-bond transmission on paths, together with its sharp five-vertex tree boundary, is not implied by the inspected sources. Searches of published mathematical records and previously available claims returned no equivalent finite-path theorem; this remains best-knowledge originality rather than a global uniqueness guarantee.
residual_risks: A preexisting theorem on path node deletion optimizing the non-singleton component probability could imply the result under alternative terminology.
The primary literature on targeted immunization is large, and only especially close works were read in full.

value.rationale: A practitioner choosing one vaccine on a chain faces two natural objectives: expected infected count and risk of any onward infection. The theorem characterizes both exactly for all path lengths and transmissibilities, identifies a sharp smallest tree where they disagree, and quantifies the five-node cost-risk tradeoff. This is a structural separation across whole parameter ranges, not a small numeric gain or an arbitrary example. Scope excludes realistic heterogeneity and correlation.
